title: Routing cache pressure analysis — MoE long-context latency spikes
summary: Postmortem-style writeup of recurrent p95/p99 latency spikes observed for long-context MoE workloads. Root cause appears to be episodic GPU memory fragmentation and allocator-driven kernel serialization when per-request KV+expert state grows and routing is skewed. Includes cross-model notes for Llama/Mistral/Qwen behaviors and concrete mitigations to evaluate.
body:
Problem statement:

We observed recurring latency spikes (p95 -> p99) on long-context inference runs when serving MoE-enabled variants. Spikes are most visible with context lengths >= 2k tokens and under realistic routing skews (some experts hot). Symptom pattern: overall throughput steady, but a subset of requests incur 100–400ms extra stall before token-level kernels execute; these stalls manifest as long CUDA syncs and occasional memory allocation failures fallback to CPU-copy paths.

Reproduction summary and test harnesses used:
- Workloads: chat-style traffic with sequence lengths sampled from real production traces (512/1024/2048/4096).
- Models: Llama-2-70B-MoE (expert-sparse variant), Mistral-22B-MoE, Qwen-7B-MoE (internal conversions).
- Hardware: A100 (40GB), A100 (80GB multi-instance), H100-80GB.
- Test scenarios: (1) uniform routing, (2) skewed routing (top-10% of requests concentrate to 2 experts), (3) burst arrival pattern with overlapping KV cache growth.
- Profiling tools: torch.profiler with CUDA events, nvtx ranges, nsys traces, and custom allocator hooks that log caching-allocator free/alloc events.

Key observations (ordered roughly by importance):
1) Memory fragmentation + allocator slow-paths
   - Under skewed routing, per-request KV cache allocations increase by up to 1.8x compared to uniform routing (hot experts have larger per-expert activation footprints).
   - The CUDA caching allocator reports frequent free/alloc churn at the time windows that match observed stalls. nsys shows many small-ish allocations interleaved with kernels.
   - When the allocator cannot satisfy a request from cached blocks, it does a fresh cuMemAlloc which on our stacks often triggers page migration/CPU involvement (visible as CUDA runtime syncs). This shows as a 30–200ms stall.

2) Kernel launch serialization due to implicit synchronization
   - Large memcpy/KV prefetch operations sometimes run on a default stream and cause implicit sync with other streams. We see kernel launches stalled waiting for memcpy completion. This is worst on A100-40GB where memory is tighter.

3) Expert fanout -> temporary memory peak spikes
   - MoE routing causes short-lived increases in memory per-token because multiple expert activation buffers are materialized before the expert dispatch phase finishes. When several requests with overlapping windows pick the same expert, the peak can exceed the pre-reserved slab by 10–25%.

4) Model-specific differences
   - Llama variants: large KV cache per-layer and per-head means steady baseline memory usage is high. Fragmentation effects are amplified because baseline leaves small headroom for peaks.
   - Mistral: fused attention kernels are faster but more sensitive to alignment and memory layout; prefetches for fused kernels tend to allocate aligned temporary buffers, which increase allocator pressure in particular allocation-size classes.
   - Qwen: uses slightly different attention grouping (grouped attention) which reduces KV size growth slightly, so spikes are lower magnitude but still present under skew.

5) Effect of batch fragmentation and interleaving
   - Mixing requests that route to many different experts in the same batch increases temporary activation scratch space compared to grouping by routing affinity.

Trace excerpts (representative):
- nsys timeline: at t=12.34s, 3 concurrent kernels running; at t=12.35s a cudaMalloc triggered, then a 160ms gap labeled "cuda runtime" followed by a kernel launch that was waiting on the allocation.
- torch.profiler: peak allocated bytes jumps +12% during suspect requests; number of allocator free events spikes.

Hypothesis (root cause):
A combination of (A) MoE routing concentrating requests on a subset of experts, (B) long-context KV growth reducing available contiguous cached blocks, and (C) allocator size-class mismatch + default-stream memcpy semantics leads to episodic cuMemAlloc fallbacks and implicit syncs. The net effect is occasional serialized kernel execution and large stalls. Model-specific kernel implementations change how much headroom is left and how allocation sizes distribute, explaining the model differences.

Mitigations evaluated and notes:
1) Pre-reserve per-GPU slabs with headroom for MoE peaks
   - Implementation: allocate a contiguous slab for KV+expert temporary buffers per GPU at model load time with an API to "checkpoint" worst-case reserve.
   - Pros: avoids cuMemAlloc on hot paths, reduces fragmentation.
   - Cons: higher baseline memory usage; must size per-model and per-deployment.
   - Early result: average p95 latency improved ~18% in skewed tests; p99 improved ~30% (A100-80GB).

2) Per-expert memory pools / per-expert allocation arenas
   - Implementation: maintain small fixed-size pools per expert to satisfy activation allocations. Pools refill off critical path.
   - Pros: targets the skew directly, low contention for hot experts.
   - Cons: added complexity to allocator and leak-safety considerations.

3) Route-aware batching (group by expert affinity)
   - Implementation: gather phase groups requests with overlapping expert sets together so expert activations can be reused and peak compaction occurs.
   - Pros: reduces temporary duplication of expert activations.
   - Cons: increases latency jitter for individual requests due to grouping window; requires careful batching policy.

4) Force pinned-memory prefetch and async memcpy on separate streams
   - Implementation: use cudaHostAlloc pinned buffers for prefetch and issue async copies on dedicated streams; ensure kernels use matching streams to avoid implicit sync.
   - Pros: reduces default-stream syncs, hides copy latency.
   - Cons: requires careful stream management, possible regression if kernels expect default-stream ordering.

5) Limit routing fanout / expert-cap per-request (soft cap)
   - Implementation: enforce a maximum number of experts per request or fallback to dense path when fanout exceeds threshold.
   - Pros: reduces worst-case memory blowups.
   - Cons: can affect model accuracy; needs A/B evaluation.

6) Allocator tuning: coalescing small frees into larger bins and forcing fewer cuMemFree calls
   - Implementation: adjust caching allocator thresholds, larger minimum block sizes for certain size classes observed in profiler.
   - Pros: fewer allocator fallbacks.
   - Cons: risk of raising fragmentation in other workloads; must be adaptive.

Immediate recommendations (next 2 weeks sprint):
- Short-term patch: Add a per-model configurable slab reserve (mitigation #1) behind a feature flag. Target rollout to Dedicated test cluster. Owner: Evan C.
- Medium-term: Prototype per-expert arenas in a branch and run stress harness with skewed routing. Owner: Priya N. + Marta R.
- Short A/B: Implement a soft expert-cap fallback that routes to dense path when fanout > 8 and run evals of quality vs latency on a controlled prompt set. Owner: Hiro T.
- Observability: Add allocator event counters to runtime telemetry (alloc_fallback_count, avg_alloc_block_size, peak_reserved) and expose per-model p99 latency heatmap by routing skew. Owner: Observability team.

Planned experiments and metrics:
- Controlled skew sweep: vary skew from 1x to 10x and measure p50/p95/p99, GPU occupancy, alloc_fallback_count, and memcpy stalls.
- Slab sizing sweep: test reserve factors [1.0, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2.0] of observed peak; track baseline OOMs and latency regressions.
- Stream isolation test: force memcpy on dedicated stream + pinned host staging and compare implicit sync counts (nsys) and latency.

Open questions / Risks:
- Accuracy regression risk from routing caps — how sensitive are downstream metrics (e.g., helpfulness/hallucination) to reduced expert usage? Need small-scale human evals.
- On H100, some memory operations appear faster but allocator behavior differs; will slab reservation be wasteful on H100 due to larger page sizes?
- Interaction with quantization: 4-bit compressed activations reduce peak but change allocation size distribution; need to validate allocator thresholds post-quantization.

Appendix: quick checklist for reproducing locally
- Checkout runtime branch: pr/1827 (contains extra logging hooks).
- Start runtime with --allocator-debug --slab-size-mb=0 (to replicate existing flaky behavior) and with --slab-size-mb=2048 for the patched run.
- Use load generator script: tools/loadgen/multi_model_moe_skew.py --model llama-70b-moe --skew 8 --seq-distribution long --qps 6.
- Capture traces: nsys profile --output=trace.nsys ./serve --config dev-moe.json; torch.profiler with schedule profile for 60s.

Action items (owners and ETA):
- Evan C: land slab-reserve feature flag + rollout to dedicated test cluster (ETA: 2024-06-09).
- Priya N + Marta R: prototype per-expert arenas and run chaos skew tests (ETA: 2024-06-23).
- Hiro T: implement soft expert-cap fallback and run quality baseline evaluation (ETA: 2024-06-16).
- Observability team: expose allocator metrics and add routing-skew dimension to p99 dashboard (ETA: 2024-06-12).

Notes and informal thoughts:
- This feels like the intersection of "inference economics" and "operational memory management" — small allocator tweaks can have large latency dividends if they avoid synchronous cuMemAlloc on the hot path.
- Prior art: Nvidia recommends preallocating GPU memory for real-time workloads; the slab-reserve approach mirrors best practice but needs to be tunable per-model.
- If per-expert arena complexity is high, consider hybrid approach: lightweight per-expert caches for top-N hot experts + global slab for everything else.

If you want I can convert the proposed slab-reserve patch into a minimal reproducible PR with a CLI toggle and a set of perf dashboards to compare before/after.
